q: Which best describes what happened in the two winters?
options: Emissions fell sharply in 2022-23, then rose sharply in 2023-24
Pollution fell everywhere in both winters
North India was dirtier than usual in both winters
North India was cleaner and the peninsula dirtier in 2022-23, then the pattern reversed in 2023-24, with no major change in emissions or policy
explain: In 2022-23 north India's PM2.5 was down by up to 30% while Mumbai rose 45%. In 2023-24 it flipped: Jaipur rose about 50% and Delhi over 10%, while the peninsula got cleaner. The study found no major change in emissions or pollution-control policy.

q: In Jaipur, what did the study find about rain and pressure?
options: In 2022-23 rain was more strongly linked to lower PM2.5. In 2023-24 surface pressure mattered more, and pollution spiked after rain
Rain cleaned the air in every year
Pressure had no effect in either winter
Rain made the air dirtier in 2022-23
explain: Rain can wash pollution out, but high pressure can trap it. This finding is about Jaipur only, not every city.

q: Delhi-NCR has relatively low local emissions one winter. What does the study suggest?
options: Its air will be clean
Its air will be dirty
Air can still turn bad if large-scale circulation stagnates, and strong winds can dilute even substantial emissions
Emissions no longer matter
explain: Low local or farm-fire emissions do not automatically guarantee cleaner air when circulation stagnates. And strong winds can disperse or divert even substantial emissions.

q: What did the climate-zone study find for northwest India between 1951-60 and 1991-2020?
options: The hot semi-arid zone shrank to less than a fifth of the region
The hot semi-arid zone grew from about a quarter of the region to a third, pushing east into Uttar Pradesh
Nothing changed
The tropical savannah zone took over most of the region
explain: An area equal to roughly 7% of the region moved into the drier zone. The tropical savannah growth was in the peninsula, where the hot semi-arid zone shrank from about 30% to 16%. The article does not report effects on crop yields.

q: Which statement does the study support?
options: El Niño always makes Delhi's air worse
Pollution-control policies have no effect
La Niña guarantees clean air in the north
The two winters show a link between weather patterns and where pollution built up, but not proof of cause, and not a forecast
explain: The authors say the correlations do not establish direct causation, cannot be extrapolated to other years, and that the two winters studied were unusual.
